method: Claude built a new generator family, layered_maze (folder mole-tunnels, shown as Mole Tunnels), from the Maze generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (the shortest time on two floors, where changing floor costs extra, so a trip through the other floor is only sometimes worth it; the state is a square plus a floor) under an original story and pictures: a mole's burrow with an upper and a lower level of tunnels drawn side by side, squares of solid earth instead of walls, and climbing allowed only where both levels have a tunnel. Level 1 puts the goal on the lower level (one climb); level 2 has a shortcut underneath that pays even with two climbs; level 3 makes climbs dearer so that about half the time staying on top wins; level 4 asks at which of four lettered squares the fastest trip climbs down; level 5 hides the climb time and asks for the longest climb that still makes the trip underneath faster. Random burrows almost never have a shortcut worth two climbs, so the generator puts a wall of earth across the upper level with one gap near an edge, places S and G on either side away from the gap, and opens a short lower tunnel under the wall; the rest of both levels is random. Every problem passes check_layered_maze.py, which rebuilds the burrow from the picture and solves it with a 0-1 breadth-first search in which a climb is a chain of one-minute links (the generator uses Dijkstra), re-derives every habit by re-running that search on a changed burrow or with changed climb costs, follows each walk and climb line of the explanation through the burrow, and for level 5 tries climb times one by one instead of using the formula. Every corrupted answer key, tag, scene, climb time, explanation ending and explanation step in the mutation trials is caught; flipping a square in both the picture and the scene is caught whenever it changes the answer. A finding from building it: the time saved by the shortcut (top steps minus steps underneath) is always even, because the grid is bipartite, so the level 5 answer is always half the saving minus one, and the climb at exactly half the saving is always a tie. The map already had ONE_SWITCH_COST from the Maze analysis with no family; this family is the first to use it, and its wording is made general.

ladder.question: down
ladder.note: G is on the lower level: find the fastest way down, and count the climb as well as the steps.

ladder.question: detour
ladder.note: S and G are both on top, and a shortcut runs underneath: going down and coming back up are two climbs.

ladder.question: compare
ladder.note: Climbs take longer: work out both ways and see whether the shortcut underneath still pays.

ladder.question: where
ladder.note: Pick the square where the fastest trip climbs down. The nearest climb spot is not always it.

ladder.question: limit
ladder.note: The climb time is unknown: find the longest climb that still makes the trip underneath faster.

misconceptions.description: Adds up the steps of the route but leaves out the minutes spent climbing between the levels.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the trip as pieces: walk, climb, walk. Every piece takes time, the climbs too.

misconceptions.description: Only thinks of changing level at the start or at the goal, not at a spot partway along the trip.
misconceptions.remediation: List every square that is tunnel on both levels. Each one is a place the trip could change level.

misconceptions.description: Treats the two levels as one map, stepping from a tunnel on one level into a tunnel on the other without climbing.
misconceptions.remediation: Keep a finger on the level the mole is on. It can only change level by climbing at a square that is tunnel on both.

misconceptions.description: Counts the straight across-and-down distance, as if the mole could walk through solid earth.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace the trip square by square through tunnel only, and count the steps you really take.

misconceptions.description: Stays on the starting level the whole way and never checks whether a trip through the other level is faster.
misconceptions.remediation: Work out both: the time staying on top, and the time with a trip through the lower level. Then compare.

misconceptions.description: Takes a shortcut through the other level even when the two climbs cost more time than the shortcut saves.
misconceptions.remediation: Add both climbs to the shortcut, then compare it with staying on one level.

misconceptions.description: Changes level at the first climb spot it reaches instead of the spot that makes the whole trip fastest.
misconceptions.remediation: For each climb spot, add up the whole trip through it. The nearest spot is not always the best.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up the square where the trip climbs down with the square where it climbs back up.
misconceptions.remediation: Follow the trip from the start. Which climb comes first?

misconceptions.description: Climbs down where the tunnel below looks handy without checking that it leads anywhere.
misconceptions.remediation: Before climbing down, follow the lower tunnel from there. Can the mole climb back up anywhere else?

misconceptions.description: Gives the value at which the two ways take exactly the same time, as if a tie were faster.
misconceptions.remediation: Try that value: do both ways take the same time? Then one is not faster than the other.

misconception_updates.description: Counts the cost of changing level only once for a trip that goes to the other level and comes back.
misconception_updates.remediation: Write the trip as pieces. A trip that goes down and comes back up climbs twice.
